result:
The proposed answer $1/6$ is wrong. The limit is $1/10$.

**Reformulation.** Identify $\{i,j\}$ with $i<j$ as the point $(i,j)$ in the grid. Moving one token one step changes exactly one coordinate by $\pm1$, and the move is allowed exactly when the target stays in the region $\{1\le i<j\le n\}$. So $T_2(P_n)$ is the subgraph of the grid $\mathbb{Z}^2$ induced by the staircase region $R_n=\{1\le i<j\le n\}$. It has $|V|=\binom n2\sim n^2/2$ vertices.

**Lower bound.** Each vertex has at most 4 neighbours (each token has at most one left and one right move). A dominating set $S$ satisfies $|S|\cdot 5\ge \sum_{s\in S}|N[s]|\ge |V|$, so
$$\gamma(T_2(P_n))\ \ge\ \frac{\binom n2}{5}\ \sim\ \frac{n^2}{10}.$$

**Upper bound.** The perfect code $C=\{(x,y)\in\mathbb{Z}^2: x+2y\equiv 0 \pmod 5\}$ partitions $\mathbb{Z}^2$ into closed neighbourhoods of size 5. Take $C\cap R_n$, which has about $n^2/10$ elements. A vertex of $R_n$ is left undominated only if its unique code centre lies outside $R_n$. Such vertices lie within distance 1 of the boundary of $R_n$, so there are $O(n)$ of them. Adding them to the set gives
$$\gamma(T_2(P_n))\ \le\ \frac{n^2}{10}+O(n).$$

Hence $\lim_{n\to\infty}\gamma(T_2(P_n))/n^2 = 1/10$.

**Why the proposed solution fails.** Its upper bound uses $S=D_0$, which has size about $n^2/6$. That is a valid dominating set but not an optimal one. Its lower-bound step ("the modular construction achieving the bound implied by the cycle's domination density") is not an argument, and the $C_3$ heuristic does not bound the domination number. The true density is governed by the grid's perfect code, not by the mod-3 classes.

VERDICT: REJECT
